title: A Judge Killed Trump's $100,000 H-1B Fee. Four Days Later, He Put His Own Ruling on Hold.
excerpt: The legal seesaw over the most disruptive visa fee in decades is far from over — and Congress is now moving to make it permanent.
body:
The $100,000 fee that upended America's flagship skilled-worker visa programme has entered a legal twilight zone. A federal judge struck it down. Then he paused his own ruling. Now a congressman wants to enshrine it in statute. For the hundreds of thousands of Indian professionals whose careers depend on the H-1B, the whiplash is the point.

## The Ruling That Briefly Changed Everything

On June 8, U.S. District Judge Leo Sorokin in Boston vacated President Trump's $100,000 fee on all new H-1B visa petitions, calling it an unconstitutional tax that only Congress has the power to levy. The ruling was sweeping: Sorokin invalidated not just the fee itself but every memorandum, guidance document, FAQ, and fee schedule the administration had used to enforce it.

"The President had no power to levy a tax on H-1B petitions," Sorokin wrote in a 42-page opinion. "The Proclamation did not carry the force of law."

The lawsuit, led by California and joined by 19 other states, argued the fee was gutting their ability to staff public universities, hospitals, and school systems. Before the proclamation, employers typically paid $2,000 to $5,000 in H-1B filing fees. The hundredfold increase had already cratered demand: as of February, only 85 employers had paid the new price.

## Four Days Later, a Reversal

The relief was short-lived. The Trump administration immediately appealed and on June 12 asked Sorokin to stay his own order while the case moves to the First Circuit Court of Appeals. Sorokin agreed. The $100,000 fee is now effectively back in force — at least until the appellate court weighs in.

Department of Justice attorneys argued the fee is a legitimate exercise of presidential authority over foreign commerce and immigration. "Every day the district court's order remains in effect, additional aliens will rush to seek classification and entry as an H-1B nonimmigrant worker," they wrote.

The stay means employers are once again on the hook for the six-figure filing cost, and the visa programme remains in its depressed state.

## Congress Steps In

The day after the ruling, Republican Rep. Mike Kennedy of Utah introduced the PROTECT Act, a bill that would codify the $100,000 fee at the congressional level — effectively rendering the constitutional objection moot. Kennedy's legislation would require H-1B applicants to pay the greater of prevailing rates or $100,000, with the explicit goal of compelling companies to hire American-born workers first.

"The ruling shows we needed somebody in Congress to actually take care of this," Kennedy told the Daily Caller News Foundation.

The bill faces an uncertain path. Democrats, who led the lawsuit to kill the fee, are unlikely to support it. But it signals the political appetite to make the fee permanent regardless of how the courts rule.

## What It Means for Indian Professionals

Indians are the largest beneficiaries of the H-1B programme, accounting for more than 70 per cent of all approved petitions annually. The $100,000 fee has functioned as a de facto ban: at that price, only the most deep-pocketed employers — the Googles and Microsofts — can afford to sponsor a visa. Smaller firms, staffing companies, universities, and hospitals have largely stopped filing.

The practical effect has been to freeze a generation of Indian tech workers, researchers, and medical professionals out of the American labour market. The fee also does not apply to visa renewals or to foreign nationals already in the country on student visas — creating a two-tier system that favours those already in the U.S. over fresh applicants from India.

Meanwhile, a separate Department of Labor proposal would require employers to pay H-1B holders up to 33 per cent more than American coworkers in the same role. The National Foundation for American Policy has called this proposal likely illegal, but it adds another layer of cost pressure.

## The Legal Road Ahead

Three separate lawsuits are now challenging the fee, including cases by the U.S. Chamber of Commerce and staffing companies. A judge in Washington, D.C., sided with the administration in December. The First Circuit's decision could come within months — but a Supreme Court challenge is increasingly likely, given the split between federal courts.

For NRIs weighing a return to the U.S. or advising family members on career moves, the signal is clear: the H-1B fee is alive, contested, and politically charged in a way it has never been before. The programme that built Silicon Valley's Indian workforce is being repriced, and neither side is backing down.

*Sources: Reuters, Bloomberg Law, Fox News, USA Today, Inc.com*
